contributions.text_english: 6. How will the Cabinet Minister ensure that gender budgeting becomes an integral part of budget development, decision making and scrutiny during this Senedd? OQ64710
contributions.text_original: 6. Sut fydd y Gweinidog Cabinet yn sicrhau bod cyllidebu rhywedd yn dod yn rhan annatod o ddatblygu, gwneud penderfyniadau a chraffu ar y gyllideb yn ystod y Senedd hon? OQ64710

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english: Diolch. I welcome that this Government is working towards its manifesto commitment to embed gender budgeting in Wales. International best practice places that responsibility for this with the Treasury—in that case, you, Minister—because budget decisions shape people's everyday lives. Gender budgeting can seem complex, so I'll attempt an everyday analogy: a good cook does not wait until the guests have eaten to find out whether their recipe worked. Tasting, or testing, happens beforehand, and Government should be no different. Gender budgeting is about assessing the impact of spending decisions before they are made, rather than discovering too late that they've deepened existing inequalities. The case in Wales is stark. Women are three times more likely than men to work part time, three and a half times more likely to be economically inactive, because of caring responsibilities, and face a gender pay gap of 11.8 per cent. So, Minister, what leadership will you show to embed gender budgeting across Government?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english: First Minister, I'm proud to support a grass-roots campaign in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg to stop the proposed small modular reactor nuclear project in the Llynfi valley by Last Energy. More extractive and harmful projects are not what our post-industrial communities deserve. It's no surprise why they have selected one of our most deprived communities to pilot this new nuclear technology. Campaigners across the constituency are calling out for renewable energy projects that they can directly benefit from, and that's why we're exploring alternative energy options within the constituency rather than accepting private organisations coming in to extract the profits from our communities. So, Prif Weinidog, will you reaffirm this Government's ambition to ensure that our communities benefit from energy projects?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Weinidog. Patients in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg tell me that they are left chasing health boards for basic information about appointments, waiting lists and treatment plans, and are sometimes given conflicting information by different parts of the NHS. Poor communication isn't limited to patients and service providers. In a recent case that I dealt with, a cancer patient was referred by their health board, Cwm Taf Morgannwg, to Swansea bay to receive a biopsy. When concerns were raised about delays in receiving their results, neither health board took any accountability to provide the update.

Does the Cabinet Minister accept that this is not simply an inconvenience, but an unacceptable failure of patient care? What action can be taken to ensure that patients are kept properly informed throughout their treatment journey?

contributions.text_english:
Prif Weinidog, as you've outlined, discussions about our international offices too often reduce them to a line in a budget, as if a desk abroad is simply a cost to be defended. But, as you said, an office is not just a desk, it's a doorway. The relationships we build with Governments and organisations overseas translate into direct benefits for the Welsh economy: trade routes opened, investment attracted, markets found for Welsh businesses, which no amount of domestic marketing can replicate. I don't know if that was an experience of the business owner, of the Member over there.

So, in an increasingly interconnected world, I believe that we must think global and act local, learning not only from our neighbours in Scotland and Ireland, but from all across the world. That's why programmes such as Taith's international learning exchanges are so important in forging those connections. So, may I ask if you agree with me, First Minister, that Welsh Government international offices should be measured not only in monetary value, but in the relationships they build—relationships that deliver real economic benefits for the people of Wales?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english: It's encouraging that the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government is on track to deliver 12.5 hours of funded childcare per week across all 22 local authorities by the end of the financial year, a commitment that Welsh Labour promised but failed to deliver in its last five-year term in Government. Ashamedly, poverty has seeped throughout our nation. Whilst Flying Start was a good starting point, the Bevan Foundation warned that relying on this framework risks unequal access and lacks the flexibility that parents need. The phrase 'postcode lottery' has become synonymous with Flying Start. Tackling poverty and inequality requires decisive action. This is why people voted for Plaid Cymru. We have a vision for childcare that actually works for families and puts money back in their pockets, when the average weekly cost of a childcare place in Wales is £290 a week, £58 more a week than in England. Will the Cabinet Minister provide more information on the timeline for rolling out the remainder of the offer and what steps are being taken to ensure equal access to the universal childcare that will tackle the cost of living?

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
contributions.text_english:
Diolch. Here in Cymru, we had a proud tradition of peace activism. Many of us can trace our family history back to a woman who signed the Welsh women's peace petition. St Fagans held a powerful exhibition tracing that journey from the women who organised for peace in the aftermath of the first world war to the women of Greenham Common who sacrificed so much in their campaign against nuclear weapons. Once again, we find ourselves living through turbulent times with devastating conflicts unfolding across the world. And, of course, there remains a pragmatic need for defence, and we must engage honestly with that reality.

I welcome the work that this Plaid Cymru Government is undertaking to develop an ethical defence investment framework. It presents a real opportunity to build on the Scottish Government's human rights due diligence approach, which evaluates businesses before they receive public grants or investment, and to establish a gold standard for ethical investment here in Wales. This framework is the first of its kind in Cymru, and Wales can be world-leading in setting clear expectations that public money should never support companies linked to human rights abuses or violations of international law. It allows us to stand on the shoulders of those women who came before us and carry forward their commitment to peace, justice and ethical leadership. Whether the conflict is in Gaza, South Sudan or Ukraine, we should be clear in our determination that no weapon manufactured, even in part, in Wales should ever be used in a way that breaches international human rights law.

Global responsibility is not just about following money. It is about ensuring Wales is never complicit in human rights abuses, and that our economic choices reflect our commitment to peace, justice and international solidarity. But we must also be honest about the wider questions this debate raises. Defence spending is often presented as an economic opportunity, but what kind of economy do we want to build here in Wales? The people of Wales elected this Plaid Cymru Government with a mandate for a different kind of economy, an economy that places our people and communities at its heart. They voted for an economic model rooted in ownership and community wealth, ensuring that wealth generated in Wales remains in Wales, building stronger communities, creating opportunity and delivering prosperity that is shared by all. If that is our ambition, then we must also ask who owns Wales's arms and defence manufacturing facilities and whose interests they serve. In many cases, ownership rests with large multinational corporations and private firms whose primary responsibility is to shareholders—

Last Friday marked International Equal Pay Day, a UN awareness day of gender inequality and the gender pay gap between men and women. Sadly, this is a pressing issue for Wales. Compared to men, women are over three times more likely to be out of the job market due to caring responsibilities. Women are also three times more likely to work part-time, which is limiting to earnings and progression. And women are more likely to work in sectors and roles that are lower paid, such as health and social care. We need change.

Women must be supported to access better paid jobs, skills and training programmes throughout their careers, and we must have robust and inclusive policies on flexible working, harassment, menopause and parental leave. contributions.text_english:
Diolch. I speak here as a representative of a recognised, protected minority group, not only for transgender and non-binary people in my own constituency, but for transgender people right across Wales. contributions.text_english:
Whilst foreign affairs and arms export licences are reserved to Westminster, decisions about how Welsh public money is spent are made here in Cymru. Plaid Cymru demonstrated leadership, acting on a long legacy of peace, leading the Senedd's endorsement for ceasefire in Gaza in 2023, the first nation to do so. This small act led to huge hope for a nation who, I assure you, felt all hope was lost. Now, in Government, Plaid Cymru can go even further by showing leadership on international human rights law.

A freedom of information request by Amnesty International found that the previous Labour Welsh Government had given £500,000 to a company supplying military components to Israel, despite assurance otherwise from the then First Minister. This shows a clear need for accountability and a more responsible way of investing in our communities, so it's reassuring to hear that this Welsh Government is committed to taking a different approach, developing this defence ethical framework, which no previous administration has done, establishing a clear and ethical approach to defence and security in Wales grounded in human rights, international law and our commitment to peace.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Reform UK Debate: Grooming gangs
contributions.text_english:
I wanted to address those who truly matter at the centre of this: the women and children who have survived group-based sexual exploitation. I want to speak to everyone who has been in a vulnerable position and let down by those in power who were meant to be there to protect them.

My mum was barely 15 when she went to her GP and told him she was pregnant. His only advice was, 'Go home and tell your parents.' She was alone, she was frightened, and she hid it. Her teachers watched and shook their heads as the gossip spread around school while she used a ribbon to extend her school skirt around her growing baby. And three weeks after turning 16, my mum gave birth, and that was the first time that she'd been properly cared for by those who should have protected her. Too often, girls like my mum are judged on their bad choices rather than seen as children who needed help. I want every survivor to know that I hear you, I see you, and I believe you. You deserve support, and you deserve justice.

Quite often, what we've heard in debates is Reform inciting fear in minority groups. What we want to do is focus on what we would do to improve lives in Wales. It's so important that that is our focus. We all wish to make sure that we treat women as equal in our society and equal in this Chamber. We wish to hear and listen to every voice.

Reform position themselves as 'outside of the establishment', which obscures its own role in maintaining the political culture where male violence flourishes. This culture starts with harmless banter and women being spoken over, but it can escalate into intimidation, harassment, abuse and sexual violence. Here in Wales, specialist violence against women, domestic abuse and sexual violence services have warned of rising demand and increasingly complex high-risk cases, reminding us that violence against women is not an abstract issue, but a daily reality for far too many.

The system is still, too often, failing to deliver justice and protection, and changing that should be our collective commitment. Safety is not a slogan, it's a priority. Group-based abusers do not respect borders. We've heard how survivors have been trafficked across the UK and into Wales and out of Wales, so it's vital that we hear from everybody who has been in our country. This ensures that perpetrators are held to account.

Plaid Cymru's amendment is the right course of action because it puts victims and survivors first. Rather than duplicating efforts with a separate inquiry, we can work within the existing statutory framework to focus on what actually makes a difference—delivering the actions of the national strategy for prevention and responding to child sexual abuse. This is how we ensure that women and girls get the justice and support that they deserve.

contributions.text_english:
Minister, the focus in this Chamber thus far has been on the cost of childcare plans, rather than on recognising childcare as a critical lever for reducing both poverty and inequality. Childcare is a complicated issue—just ask any parent attempting to fill out an eligibility form—but it's essential economic and social infrastructure. And this is where we, across the political spectrum, must scrutinise your work. This policy will reduce child poverty and support women who've been forced out of the workplace by the motherhood penalty, which impacts everything from your pay packet to your pension. We saw on the doorstep how many people cared about this issue, which is why they voted for Plaid Cymru in their droves.

The UK Labour Government took their eye off the ball, which is why we've ended up with the most expensive childcare, here in Wales, across the UK, and why parents have said to me that they're moving out of Wales simply to make ends meet. Twenty-seven million pounds was reallocated out of the childcare budget in the last term, along with £140 million in Barnett consequentials that were lost due to the expansion of childcare in England. GDP doesn't show whether childcare is affordable, whether women working in our foundational sectors are paid fairly, whether the services and community infrastructure that they rely on are being strengthened. It doesn't reflect the unpaid care work that mostly women do, or whether economic power sits within our communities rather than elsewhere. As you establish this new development agency, will you commit to measuring success in ways that reflect real improvements in people's lives—in fair work, investment in care, stronger local supply chains, and more locally rooted, socially responsible business growth? How will you ensure that the growth that we pursue delivers genuine economic security for communities in Wales, rather than simply increasing our GDP? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
contributions.text_english: As a self-professed bibliophile, I very much welcome the manifesto commitment for a library in every primary school. Schemes such as Bookstart by BookTrust Cymru help parents read with babies and toddlers, ensuring the youngest in society have access to the opportunities that they deserve from the very start. I'd like to ask how you'll work with organisations like BookTrust Cymru to ensure all children have access to such schemes before starting school, so that their opportunities are not limited before they enter formal education?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
contributions.text_english:
The Commission does set high standards and they're grounded in the Nolan principles and in our duty to respect dignity and equality. These principles underpin public confidence in Government, which is why maintaining high standards is essential, but that's only half the battle. Embedding them in day-to-day practice is where public trust is won or lost. Training cannot be a passive tick-box exercise. It must be an active, continuous commitment to sustaining confidence in our democracy, not only in the standards we hold each other to, but in the standards the public rightly expect of us. These principles must be lived throughout every term, not simply acknowledged at induction. 

Transparency and robust accountability are equally important. Without rigorous oversight, these principles risk becoming words on paper rather than behaviours in practice. Upholding high standards is a serious responsibility and it cannot be taken lightly. I recognise the training provision outlined, but could the Member clarify how the Commission assesses its impact on behaviour and on upholding the integrity of the Senedd?

contributions.text_english:
I welcome the Deputy First Minister's response to the tragic events. This morning, I spoke with Miguel Delgado, who went two days without hearing from his mother in La Guaira before finally learning she was alive but had lost her home, and that his cousin and her three-year-old child had tragically died. Our condolences go out to all families who have lost loved ones. Miguel has been embraced by his local community, and he spoke about the similarities between La Guaira and Wales, places where everyone knows each other, they support each other and they rally together in crisis.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Stillbirth and neonatal mortality
contributions.text_english:
During the COVID pandemic, I led the Welsh part of the But Not Maternity campaign. We exposed the profound unfairness of families being separated at the most vulnerable moments of pregnancy, birth and loss. It was a time when you could still sit in the pub in a small group, but partners were barred from being present for labour, scans or devastating news.

There is one family who contacted me that I will never forget: a mother who was in hospital awaiting a medical procedure after losing her baby. Her partner, the baby's father, was not allowed to be with her because of the COVID restrictions. They were both heartbroken, both alone, and all they wanted to do was hold each other in their grief. That kind of experience leaves scars. It's not something that you can simply recover from, and it's why compassionate, consistent mental health support must be a core part of baby loss care, not an optional extra.

We must also remember the parents whose babies arrive far too early. Families with premature babies often spend weeks or months in neonatal units, living in a state of constant fear and exhaustion. Many describe the trauma of watching their tiny baby fight for life whilst navigating employment, limited visiting and the emotional whiplash of good days followed by terrifying setbacks. Neonatal care saves lives, but the emotional toll on parents is immense, particularly parents leaving those units without their precious babies. These parents need structured psychological support not just in the moment, but long after they leave the unit.

I also want to recognise a Bridgend constituent, Mark Williams, who has led the How Are You, Dad? campaign. His work reminds us that dads and all non-birthing parents experience trauma too, whether through baby loss, premature birth or the long weeks of neonatal care. Their mental health matters, their grief is real, and their inclusion in support services is essential for the well-being of the whole family. If we are serious about preventing long-term trauma, then mental health support must be embedded throughout maternity, neonatal and bereavement pathways, accessible, timely and offered to every parent, not only those who know how to ask.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Reform UK Debate: Government international spending
contributions.text_english:
I would like to declare an interest, that, in my previous role, I was chair of Wales Overseas Agencies Group, spokesperson for Disasters Emergency Committee Cymru, and, in the past, I have been sponsored by the Rotary Club of Llantwit Major to undertake a global study exchange in the Philippines.

This motion calls on the Welsh Government to end all international spending. It asks us to turn our backs on the world, to close the door on our values and to sever the ties of solidarity that have long defined Wales. I urge Members to reject the politics of division and hate.

Our global connections are no further away than a glance out of the window above us towards Tiger Bay, but let us not romanticise that, because those docks were arteries of empire, loading ships with resources extracted through colonial exploitation. We must remember that history with clear eyes. Yet Welsh people—our trade unions, our faith groups, our communities—have always sought a different path. From the women's peace petition of 1924 to our status as the world's first Fairtrade Nation, we have chosen to use our global connections for good, not for greed. To scrap international spending is to betray that tradition. It's to signal that Wales no longer cares.

So, let us look at what this spending actually achieves. The Welsh Government, along with all other UK nations, have supported the Disasters Emergency Committee, and DEC appeals launched in response to some of the world's worst humanitarian disasters are literally life-saving—food, water, medical care and shelter for people suffering unimaginable hardship. And in recent years, sadly, we have seen a plethora of humanitarian crises: the distress of Ukrainian citizens in response to the Russian invasion; the harrowing scenes of the Turkey-Syria earthquake, when families watched rescue teams digging their loved ones from under rubble; the dystopian horrors of a genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza. And I was always humbled that, despite how little many people in Wales have, they always answered the DEC's calls for support.

Natural disasters, pandemics and conflicts rarely respect borders. But co-operation and learning crosses borders too, and that is something that we can all gain from. This argument for isolation is a false one. It suggests that, by looking inward, we become stronger. But I'm still waiting for an example of a Brexit benefit. In a world facing climate change, conflict and inequality, no nation is an island. The challenges faced abroad are often the precursors to the challenges that we face at home. The COVID pandemic, the cost-of-living crisis, the inflation in our fuel bills—these are reminders that our economies and our societies are intertwined. I know the lifelong benefits of programmes like Taith, enabling learners from every part of Wales to travel to more than 90 countries, broadening horizons that no classroom alone can reach. This is not wasteful spending. It's a prudent investment in our shared future.

Some try to paint Plaid Cymru as separatists, using semantics to spread division, rather than focus on real scrutiny. But we, Plaid Cymru, stick to our values. We are internationalists. We believe in a Wales that opens a hand of friendship, because there truly is a welcome in the hillside. I urge Members to reject this motion. Let us reaffirm our commitment to a Wales that leads not just in policy like the Well-being of Future Generations Act 2015, but in action. Let us continue to stand with people in need, to build partnerships, and for our small nation to lead the work for a more just and peaceful world. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Reform UK Debate: Childcare offer
contributions.text_english:
Let us not forget that Reform UK's entire Senedd manifesto contained nothing on childcare at all—not a single proposal. At a time when families across Wales are struggling, this omission speaks volumes about their priorities. Of course, it's mainly women who are paying the price for inadequate childcare provision, with mothers forced to reduce their working hours or leave work entirely in order to care for their children. As a result, women are pushed into a vicious cycle of poverty, with years spent in the employment wilderness, followed by a lifetime of earning less in less senior roles than men, and ultimately facing a pension black hole because of prolonged periods without earnings. This is the societal cost of failing to take childcare seriously.

Reform UK's proposed tax breaks would do nothing to support parents who've already been forced out of the workforce because their childcare bills outweigh their earnings. Through my volunteer work, leading campaigns with Pregnant then Screwed, I've spoken to hundreds of families across Wales—families taking out credit cards simply to cover their childcare bills. That's the reality that Reform chooses to ignore.

We've also heard Reform representatives, including Dan Thomas, speak to the BBC about improving maternity and paternity rights. Yet this sits in direct contradiction to Reform UK's own policy of scrapping the Equality Act 2010. Removing the Equality Act would wipe out decades of progress on workplace rights and leave thousands of women without legal protection, if they were pushed out of their jobs for becoming pregnant or for taking maternity leave like I was.

Reform candidates have also chosen to spread fear and misinformation about the childcare sector, claiming that abuse in nurseries will skyrocket if parents are offered more funded childcare hours, adding that mothers will wish they'd looked after their babies themselves. This is misogyny and fearmongering, plain and simple. It insults both childcare professionals and parents. Claims that children in nursery are at risk of abuse are not only baseless, but deeply damaging. They undermine the professionalism and dedication of expert childcare staff. Nursery workers and child minders are a vital part of our care economy, and they ensure that our children have the best possible start in life, and these comments do a profound disservice to a sector already under immense pressure.

In 2024, I founded and chaired the childcare expert group. With Oxfam Cymru, I commissioned detailed research into the true cost of delivering high-quality childcare here in Wales. And that work has given me full confidence that Wales can deliver the transformational childcare offer that families have needed for far too long. Plaid Cymru believes in this ambitious approach, one rooted in evidence, fairness and the well-being of families. Expanding access to high-quality childcare is not only about supporting parents; it's about tackling poverty, supporting our economy, achieving equality and ensuring the best future for our children. Diolch.
